content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary & Pros
- This paper proposes a transfer learning approach based on fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. This approach adaptively computes the importance weights of classes in the source dataset, for maximizing the transfer effect.
- The authors consider the importance weight as an action, and evaluation on the validation set as a reward. Using this formulation, they learn a policy network (i.e., importance weight) via policy gradient. This scheme does not require explicit similarity metrics between source and target samples.
- The proposed method outperforms fine-tuning and DATL in several settings.

Concerns #1: Verification of RL-based approach
- Policy gradient algorithms should update policy networks to maximize the Q-value function. However, the proposed method considers maximizing only an instant reward at the current iteration in a greedy manner. Also, a number of episodes are typically required for learning while the proposed method considers only one episode. Thus it is hard to guarantee that policy gradient can find a good policy.
- I think this method is more related to gradient approximation of objective (R) than RL because the advantage A_t can be considered as R(theta_t+1)-R(theta_t), so the gradient might be approximated as A_t*dP(lambda)/dtheta_t.
- In Algorithm 1, computing lambda is deterministic. However, REINFORCE is based on stochastic policy. So I wonder how to apply REINFORCE into the proposed framework more precisely.
- Detailed ablation studies on RL-based importance weights should be provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of RL, e.g., weight distribution while training, or using multi-step rewards instead of instant (or one-step) rewards.

Concerns #2: Novelty of the proposed method
- I think the novelty seems to be limited because the proposed method just trains class-wise importance weights using the validation set.
- For training the weights, the proposed method uses REINFORCE without any modification to specialize this problem, thus I think this paper has a limited contribution.

Concerns #3: Incremental improvements
- The performance gains of L2TL over fine-tuning seem to be incremental even many samples in the source dataset are irrelevant to the target task (Table 1 & 4). I think ImageNet has many irrelevant samples to the fine-grained tasks, e.g., ImageNet has a small number of bird-related class.
- For each target task, the proposed method requires all samples (>100GB) in the source dataset while fine-tuning just needs pre-trained models (< 100MB). Despite the high complexity, the performance gain is relatively small.
- When fine-tuning, a regularization technique can also provide meaningful improvements on such fine-grained datasets, e.g., MaxEnt [1].
- Overall, to prove the effectiveness of the proposed method, I think it should provide more improvements.

[1] Dubey, Abhimanyu, et al. "Maximum-Entropy Fine Grained Classification." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2018.

content.title: Response to Review #3  - part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for appreciating our technical contributions and providing suggestions to improve our paper. 

Concerns #1: Verification of RL-based approach

“- Policy gradient algorithms should update policy networks to maximize the Q-value function. However, the proposed method considers maximizing only an instant reward at the current iteration in a greedy manner. Also, a number of episodes are typically required for learning while the proposed method considers only one episode. Thus it is hard to guarantee that policy gradient can find a good policy.”

Response: 
Empirically, we observe that using an instant reward works sufficiently well. In principle, we can sample multiple weights from the policy at each episode. In Algorithm 1, we sample multiple ($B_T$)  data samples from the target validation set. Thus, the rewards are obtained from multiple samples for each update. So we basically leverage multiples episodes for learning. Based on the rewards, the source class weights are updated directly, instead of a policy network to update them. Note that the source class weights are shared among different episodes, and the actions eventually determine their final value based on the guidance with the rewards. Our approach can find a good policy eventually, as evident from the performance results. We will clarify this in the paper.

“- I think this method is more related to gradient approximation of objective (R) than RL because the advantage A_t can be considered as R(theta_t+1)-R(theta_t), so the gradient might be approximated as A_t*dP(lambda)/dtheta_t.”

Response: 
Instead of introducing any gradient approximation to the objective, our method directly outputs the action that would guide towards the $\lambda$ to achieve the optimal reward value. We leverage REINFORCE to compute the gradient for $\lambda$, while the convolutional weights are optimized by standard gradient descent. We also note that the reward can be a non-differentiable objective like AUC.

“- In Algorithm 1, computing lambda is deterministic. However, REINFORCE is based on stochastic policy. So I wonder how to apply REINFORCE into the proposed framework more precisely.”

Response:
In Section 4, we already explained that $\lambda$ is sampled from the learned policy in a stochastic way. We will also introduce this step in Algorithm 1 for clarity. 

“- Detailed ablation studies on RL-based importance weights should be provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of RL, e.g., weight distribution while training, or using multi-step rewards instead of instant (or one-step) rewards.”

We already have Fig. 3 on the effectiveness of RL-based importance weights. We will also include a plot on the evolution of weights.

Concerns #2: Novelty of the proposed method

Response:
Our motivation of incorporating reinforcement learning for reweighting source examples is novel as it is the first time reinforcement-learning based policy is integrated for the purpose of optimal information extraction from a source dataset. We agree that we use the REINFORCE algorithm in its conventional form, but we formulate transfer learning with a novel objective. In this new objective, not only do we train class-wise importance weights, but we also consider a dataset relevance score to measure the global similarities. Overall, application of RL to the fundamental problem of transfer learning is novel, and our paper demonstrates strong results for it on a wide range of cases.

Concerns #3: Incremental improvements

“- The performance gains of L2TL over fine-tuning seem to be incremental even many samples in the source dataset are irrelevant to the target task (Table 1 & 4). I think ImageNet has many irrelevant samples to the fine-grained tasks, e.g., ImageNet has a small number of bird-related class.”

Response:

Please note that with a strong network and learning rate scheduling, fine-tuning is a solid baseline for the datasets in Table 1 (Cui et al., 2018). We agree that ImageNet has many irrelevant samples to the fine-grained tasks but at the same time, there is a lot of pattern sharing between images from even very different types of classes, that’s why fine-tuning is already effective even when it is applied on completely unrelated target datasets (e.g. when the source dataset is ImageNet and the target dataset is a medical diagnosis datasets). 

The improvement of L2TL comes from judicious selection of relevant classes from the ImageNet dataset to facilitate generalization on target datasets, and can be significant in many cases, up to 1.3% in fine-tuning with the entire dataset, up to 6.5% relative accuracy gain in low-shot regime, and up to 7.5% when a larger-scale source dataset is considered.

content.title: Response to Review #3 - part 2
content.comment:
“- For each target task, the proposed method requires all samples (>100GB) in the source dataset while fine-tuning just needs pre-trained models (< 100MB). Despite the high complexity, the performance gain is relatively small.”

Response:

Firstly, please refer to the above paragraph regarding how high the performance gains could be in different regimes. The storage amount to represent source dataset is a drawback for L2TL as indicated, as training of L2TL requires the entire source dataset. We will mention this in our updated paper. However, we would like to emphasize that the computational complexity is a different aspect than storage amount. We provide comparisons to fine-tuning in terms of training speed in Section 6 and indeed we show that the amount of difference is small - roughly 30%, not orders of magnitude difference as indicated.  

“- When fine-tuning, a regularization technique can also provide meaningful improvements on such fine-grained datasets, e.g., MaxEnt [1].”

We will add a citation for this work. It is possible to integrate such regularization techniques inside L2TL framework to further improve performance which we leave to future work.

We hope that we have fully addressed your questions and concerns. Please let us know if you have further comments.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
The submission is proposing an importance weighting based transfer learning algorithm in which the importance weights are learned using reinforcement learning. The reward function used in the work is the evaluation accuracy. Moreover, the learned parameters are class-based importance weights.

* Novelty *: The paper is somewhat novel. The idea of re-weighting source dataset for a better transfer has been known, and used in the literature of domain adaptation well over a decade (eg. Daume&Marcu JAIR 2006). The main contribution of the paper is learning these weights using reinforcement learning. However, a similar approach of learning to re-weight examples using validation rewards has been published by (Ren et al, ICML 2018). Hence, only novel contribution is extending these meta-learning the weights idea into transfer learning setting. In other words, submission combines existing ideas in a sensible way. This is definitely interesting. On the other hand, it is also important to note that the novelty is very-limited. 

* Experimental Setup *: Authors perform very extensive collection of experiments. Unfortunately, the results are neither conclusive nor complete due to following issues:

1)  It is a widely known fact that reinforcement learning algorithms have huge variance. Especially, the REINFORCE method has no internal variance reduction mechanism. Considering this potential very high variance, all tables and figures need sensitivity analysis. Authors state that the experiments are run with 3 random seeds. Not reporting variances and min/max values of obtained results is clearly unacceptable. Considering the fact that all of the margins are very low, I do not find any of the results conclusive without a sensitivity analysis. More importantly, a separate sensitivity analysis to the hyper-parameters would also be very beneficial since RL is typically very hyper-parameter dependent. 

2) Baselines are incomplete. The paper is performing various experiments on both transfer learning and few-shot learning. The experiments do not include any few-shot learning baselines. Instead, it only compares with fine-tuning. Hence, the conclusion stated in the paper "...The results show that L2TL can yield significant improvements in real-world tasks where the number of training examples are limited..." is not really warranted. Transfer learning experiments are also missing various baselines. A simple baseline would be metric learning as demonstrated by Scott et al in NeurIPS 2018 (Adapted Deep Embeddings: A Synthesis of Methods for k-Shot Inductive Transfer Learning). They show that fine-tuned metric learning is a strong transfer learning baseline. Comparing only with basic fine-tuning is definitely incomplete empirical design.

* Is RL really needed? * To me, using RL for learning the weights is the real contribution of the paper. However, it is not really evaluated. There are various ways to pose this meta-learning problem and RL is only one of the ways. There are various existing methods which the paper can compare with in order to justify the RL decision. A comparison with (Ren et al., ICML 2018) is the most obvious one and can be applied in a straight-forward manner. One can replace the validation set (which is used for meta-training) with the target validation set and simply apply their method. Similarly, (Deep Bilevel Learning by Jenni et al, ECCV 2018) can be applied in a similar fashion.

content.title: Response to Review #2 - part 1
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable comments that have helped to improve the quality of our paper.

1. Novelty.

Response: 
To start with, we appreciate that you find that extending meta-learning the weights idea to transfer learning setting is interesting. We would like to further explain our perspectives on why our work contains high novelty.

To compare with our work, we present some recent works on re-weighting samples in the Related Work section. Among these, Ren et al. focuses on the task of reweighting noisy data, using gradient descent-based meta learning. On the other hand, we formulate the transfer learning problem with a new loss function, including class-relevant weights and a dataset-relevant weights. In addition, Ren et al. uses sub-gradient to update the weights of the input data. In our method, on the other hand, the weight assignments are learned with reinforcement learning, in a setting where actions are directly guided with the rewards. The reward in our approach can be a direct measure of performance and is not used to guide the weights with gradient-descent based optimization as in Ren et al.. Thus, our framework is more applicable to scenarios where the evaluation metric on the target data is non-differentiable, e.g., AUC for the CheXpert dataset. Generalization of re-weighting to transfer learning scenario is not trivial - as the framework needs to consider alternating training on source and target datasets, while defining the objective separately for the two tasks. L2TL substantially differs from the previous work in terms of motivations, technical approaches and capabilities. Thus, we believe the application of meta learning, particularly with reinforcement learning, should warrant novelty, especially given the significance of the canonical problem of transfer learning. 

2. “huge variance of reinforcement learning algorithms.”

Response: 
In Figure. 3, we show that our training algorithm can converge to the final result in the last few thousand iterations, although a larger variance is observed at the beginning of training. Note that we do not train the whole network with REINFORCE - REINFORCE is only used to train the coefficients $\Phi$, while the network weights are optimized using standard stochastic gradient descent (please refer to Algorithm 1 for details). Thus, the observations from the widely known use cases would not apply and indeed we do not observe large variations with different experimental runs. When the classifiers of both the source and the target dataset converge, the small variations in the weights for each example would not heavily affect the final performance. We have run some of the L2TL experiments with three different random seeds, and obtained the standard deviation for the accuracy around 0.1%, much smaller than the gap between different methods.

3. “baselines are incomplete”.

Response: 
First, besides fine-tuning, we also compare our method to the state-of-the-art transfer learning approaches. Our goal with low-shot experiments is to demonstrate how much the performance gap would change with the decrease in the target dataset size. 

Our low-shot experiment setting is different to the conventional few-shot learning literature, that employs N-way k-shot learning with episodic training and evaluates performances on novel categories. Besides, an external large source dataset is not used in conventional few-shot learning. Thus, we do not think the comparison would not be very relevant, but we think it could be interesting for future work, after adapting the few-shot learning setting to learn from the source dataset in a scalable way, while considering all the target classes at each iteration.

Thank you for bringing the paper by Scott et al. to our attention. Their approach is definitely interesting and promising, but does not seem computationally feasible to scale to the complexities of the models and the sizes of the datasets we consider in our paper, thus it would not be a direct competitor to L2TL or DATL when the real-world use cases are considered. Yet, we will include an experiment in their small-scale source and target dataset setting to see how our approach would compare to theirs.

content.title: Response to Review #2 - part 2
content.comment:
4. “Is RL really needed?”

Response: 
First and foremost, we demonstrate superior transfer learning performance with RL, compared to other alternative approaches. Our motivations to use RL are inspired by its successful applications in finding the optimal policy by utilizing the feedback on an action in very high dimensional and constrained search spaces.

The paper by Ren et al. does not consider transfer learning and it is not straightforward to generalize their gradient-descent based meta learning idea to reweight the source classes.  Unfortunately, it is not as simple as the approach suggested by the Reviewer: “One can replace the validation set (which is used for meta-training) with the target validation set and simply apply their method.” because there is a joint learning from the source and target training datasets, and meta weight updates should be reflected to only source classes while sharing the vast majority of the parameters between the model for the source and the target. Thus, we leave the approach of gradient-descent based meta learning to improve transfer learning to future work. Similarly, bilevel formulation can also be generalized to transfer learning, but various concerns would arise how to prioritize alignment of gradients from source vs. target dataset.

Overall, L2TL based on RL yields strong results to improve transfer learning, with manageable increase in complexity while scaling to very large scale datasets. If any other meta learning method could be proposed as a competitive transfer learning method, with strong performance improvements on the target tasks while obtaining computationally-feasible scaling to large-scale source datasets, we believe it would be a significant research contribution, rather than straightforward extensions of the papers mentioned. 

We hope that we have fully addressed your questions and concerns. Please let us know if you have further comments.
